Bottom five bracket RATES (3.90/4.40/5.15/5.40/5.90%) are read directly off the official NYS-50-T-NYS (1/26) withholding tables (NY Dept. of Taxation & Finance, effective payrolls 1/1/2026-12/31/2026), which state on page 3 these reflect rate reductions enacted under Chapter 59 of the Laws of 2025, Part A; the pre-recapture segments of that same document's Method II 'Annual Tax Rate Schedule' independently reproduce these same five rates at these same thresholds, cross-confirming them. Chapter 59 Part A changed rates only, not thresholds, so the bracket dollar breakpoints and the unchanged top four rates (6.85% above $215,400, 9.65% above $1,077,550, 10.3% above $5,000,000, 10.9% above $25,000,000) are carried forward from the 2025 IT-201-I return schedule (tax.ny.gov) with no 2026 IT-201 instructions yet published (expected late 2026/early 2027, since a tax-year-2026 return is filed in 2027) - this is a normal publication-timing gap, not a sign the 2026 rates are unconfirmed. Raised to 'verified' this pass since both bottom-five rates and all thresholds are now corroborated directly against a 2026-dated state document. Married Filing Jointly and Qualifying Surviving Spouse share one bracket table; Single and Married Filing Separately share another. New York City levies its own separate progressive resident income tax (roughly 3.078%-3.876%) and Yonkers imposes a resident income tax surcharge (16.75% of NYS tax) plus a nonresident earnings tax; neither is folded into the state brackets above. High-income NY filers are also subject to a 'benefit recapture' computation (tax computation worksheets, and reflected as non-monotonic segment rates within the withholding formula tables) that claws back the value of lower brackets above roughly $107,650 of income, separate from the clean marginal schedule shown here. Standard deduction figures ($8,000 single/MFS, $16,050 MFJ, $11,200 HOH) are the 2025 IT-201-I amounts; NY's standard deduction has been statutorily fixed since 2018 with no COLA, so no 2026 change is expected, but no 2026-dated publication states the figure explicitly. NY Paid Family Leave employee rate (0.432% of wages, capped at $411.91/year, implying a $95,349 wage base) is directly confirmed via paidfamilyleave.ny.gov's 2026 page; NY DBL (0.5% up to $0.60/week, i.e. a $6,240 annual wage base) is New York's long-standing statutory maximum, unchanged for decades.

states.name: Connecticut
states.notes: RE-VERIFIED for tax year 2026 directly: CT DRS's own IP 2026(1), 'Circular CT, Connecticut Employer's Tax Guide' (issued 12/12/2025, replaces IP 2025(1)), together with TPG-211, '2026 Withholding Calculation Rules' (Rev. 12/25), explicitly state on their first page that 'the 2026 withholding calculation rules and 2026 withholding tables are unchanged from 2025.' That is a direct, dated confirmation that these rates and thresholds are correct for tax year 2026, not merely an assumption that a form numbered for 2026 doesn't yet exist (the CT-1040 TCS return-instruction booklet for tax year 2026 indeed will not be published until late 2026/early 2027, since a 2026 return is filed in 2027, but the withholding guide is the right document to check and it confirms no change). Confidence raised from 'probable' to 'verified' this pass; CT's bracket structure and rates have been stable since the 2023 rate cut. Single and Married Filing Separately share one bracket table ('Table B: Single or Married Filing Separately' / withholding codes A/D/F); shown identically for both statuses above. CT layers TWO distinct recapture/clawback mechanisms on top of the marginal brackets: (1) Table C, '2% Tax Rate Phase-Out Add-Back' - adds back up to $250 (single/MFS), $500 (MFJ/QSS), or $400 (HOH) of tax for filers above roughly $56,500/$100,500/$78,500 Connecticut AGI, phasing out the benefit of the bottom 2% bracket; (2) Table D, 'Tax Recapture' - adds back up to $3,400 (single/MFS), $6,800 (MFJ/QSS), or $5,320 (HOH) of tax for filers above roughly $540,000/$1,080,000/$864,000 Connecticut AGI, phasing out the benefit of the 4.5%-6.9% brackets so that very-high-income filers are taxed at close to a flat 6.99% on all income. CT has NO standard deduction; instead it uses an income-based Personal Exemption (Table A, up to $15,000 single/$24,000 MFJ/$12,000 MFS/$19,000 HOH, phasing to $0 by roughly $44,000/$62,000/$35,000/$56,000 AGI) plus a separate Personal Tax Credit percentage (Table E, up to 75%) applied against computed tax based on AGI; neither is represented in the standardDeduction field (omitted). CT Paid Leave employee contribution rate (0.5% of wages) is unchanged for 2026 per the CT Paid Leave Authority; its wage base equals the federal Social Security/OASDI contribution and benefit base, confirmed by SSA to be $184,500 for calendar year 2026 (up from $176,100 in 2025).
sources: https://portal.ct.gov/drs (IP 2026(1), Circular CT, Connecticut Employer's Tax Guide, issued 12/12/2025, and TPG-211, 2026 Withholding Calculation Rules, Rev. 12/25)

states.name: Massachusetts

payrollPrograms.name: Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) - employee-side share (medical 0.28% + family 0.18%)

states.notes: Flat 5% rate applies to most wage/ordinary income (short-term capital gains and most interest/dividends are taxed at 8.5%; long-term gains on collectibles at 12% - not modeled here since this record covers wage income). A separate 4% 'millionaires tax' surtax applies on top of the 5% rate to income above an inflation-adjusted threshold, giving a combined ~9% marginal rate above that line. The threshold was $1,083,150 for tax year 2025 and rises to $1,107,750 for tax year 2026 (a routine annual inflation adjustment; mass.gov's own DOR pages, including its Technical Information Release setting this figure, returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch again this pass, so the $1,107,750 figure is corroborated across multiple third-party payroll/benefits advisory sources rather than read directly off mass.gov - kept at 'probable' rather than 'verified' for that reason, but no longer an unconfirmed carried-forward 2025 number). Massachusetts has no standard deduction; it instead uses a personal exemption (approx. $4,400 single / $8,800 MFJ, per recent-year figures) which this schema has no field for, so standardDeduction is reported as 0 for all statuses - do not treat that as 'no relief', treat it as 'not modeled in this shape.' PFML: DFML's announced 2026 total contribution rate is 0.88% of eligible wages (unchanged since 2024); for employers with 25+ covered individuals the employee-side share is capped at 0.28% (of the 0.70% medical-leave contribution) plus 0.18% (all of the family-leave contribution) = 0.46% employee-side, matching the rate below; employees at employers below the 25-count threshold still owe the same 0.46%. The wage base is assumed to equal the 2026 Social Security taxable maximum ($184,500, since MA ties the PFML cap to it), corroborated by the same third-party sources but still not independently confirmed against ssa.gov or mass.gov directly (both blocked automated fetch), so this figure remains 'probable'.

states.name: Maryland
states.notes: RE-VERIFIED this pass against a government document: the Maryland General Assembly Department of Legislative Services' Fiscal and Policy Note for HB 352 (Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act of 2025, 2025 Regular Session) spells out the exact 'before' and 'under the bill' rate tables, confirming the brackets and rates below (Exhibit 3 of that note). HB 352 added two new top brackets - 6.25% and 6.50% - above the prior 5.75% top rate, applicable 'to tax year 2025 and beyond' (so unchanged and still in effect for tax year 2026); it also raised the standard deduction's maximum value from $2,800/$5,600 (2025-prior law) to $3,350 single-MFS/$6,700 joint-HOH for tax year 2025, 'subject to annual cost-of-living adjustments for tax years after 2025' - meaning the true 2026 maximum is somewhat higher than $3,350/$6,700, but the exact COLA-adjusted 2026 figure was not located this pass, so treat these two numbers as a 2026 floor, not the exact ceiling. Maryland publishes two rate schedules, not four: Single and Married Filing Separately share one table; Married Filing Jointly, Head of Household, and Qualifying Widow(er) share the other - the duplication above is intentional, not an omission. Every Maryland county (plus Baltimore City) levies its own local income tax on top of the state brackets shown here, currently ranging roughly 2.25% to 3.20% (increased from a 3.2% cap to 3.3% by the same HB 352, for counties that elect it) depending on county of residence; this is why take-home pay differs sharply by county even at identical state income and is not incorporated into the brackets above. Maryland's standard deduction is actually computed as 15% of Maryland AGI, subject to a floor and ceiling that differ by filing group; the values reported here are the ceiling (maximum) amounts that apply once income is high enough - lower-income filers get a smaller, income-scaled deduction, not modeled in this single-number field. Maryland's FAMLI (Family and Medical Leave Insurance) program remains pre-contribution as of mid-2026: paidleave.maryland.gov states benefits launch 'starting January 2028,' and contributions (which normally precede benefits by roughly a year under this program's design) have not begun, so no employee-side payroll program is listed; re-verify before assuming this stays true into 2027. Confidence raised from 'probable' to 'verified' given the direct legislative fiscal-note confirmation, even though marylandtaxes.gov / marylandcomptroller.gov's own pages (now migrated to a ServiceNow-based portal, services.marylandcomptroller.gov) remained unreadable to automated fetch this pass (403s, 404s on stale marylandtaxes.gov links, and a JS-rendered SPA on the new portal with no usable server-rendered text).

states.name: Maine

payrollPrograms.name: Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML)

states.notes: Single and Married Filing Separately share one identical bracket table on Maine Revenue Services' official 2026 schedule (titled 'Single Individuals and Married Persons Filing Separate Returns'). Thresholds are inflation-indexed annually per 36 M.R.S. sec.5403 (COLA factors 1.303 applied to bracket floors, 1.298 to bracket ceilings for 2026). A 2% income tax surcharge applies to Maine taxable income above $1,000,000 (single), $750,000 (MFS), or $1,500,000 (MFJ/HOH) beginning tax year 2026 - not reflected in the bracket table above, which is pre-surcharge. Maine also allows a $5,300 personal exemption per taxpayer (and spouse if MFJ), on top of the standard deduction, plus additional age/blindness amounts. Do not use this table for wage withholding, which uses separate MRS withholding tables. PFML: total contribution is 1% of wages for employers with 15+ employees (up to half, i.e. 0.5%, may be deducted from employee pay) or 0.5% for employers with <15 employees (who may deduct the entire 0.5% from employee pay); the employee-side rate is capped at 0.5% of wages either way. Wage base equals the federal Social Security Administration's annual taxable wage base ($184,500 for 2026), which is set by the SSA, not Maine, and changes yearly. Payroll contributions began January 1, 2025; benefits became payable May 1, 2026.

states.notes: Bracket figures come from a Vermont CPA firm's published 2026 tax-planning tables, whose Vermont individual-rate section is explicitly labeled '(ESTIMATED)' by the preparer. Every attempted fetch of tax.vermont.gov (main personal income tax page, the '/individuals/personal-income-tax/rates' page, and the '2026-vt-rate-schedules' document URL) returned HTTP 403, so the figures could not be cross-checked directly against the primary source in this session. Internal consistency check: Married Filing Separately thresholds are exactly half of Married Filing Jointly thresholds at every breakpoint (39,975/96,650/147,300 = half of 79,950/193,300/294,600), which matches Vermont's standard bracket-splitting convention and supports the figures; the same CPA-firm table also contained an unexplained sub-breakpoint at $75,000-ish levels within same-rate bands that did not correspond to an actual rate change and was collapsed out of the reported thresholds. Vermont also indexes a $5,100 per-person personal exemption (separate from the standard deduction shown above). Vermont does NOT have a mandatory, employee-funded paid-leave payroll tax: it operates a voluntary Family and Medical Leave Insurance program (VT-FMLI, expanded to private employers with 2+ employees in July 2024) funded by an employer contribution of 0.55% of wages (up to 200% of the SSA wage base), with employers required to cover at least 50% of that contribution and any employee-side share left to employer discretion - so no employee payroll program is listed. Given the 'ESTIMATED' label and inaccessible primary source, treat these bracket/deduction numbers as needing direct verification against a live tax.vermont.gov page before use in any authoritative context.

states.name: New Hampshire
states.notes: New Hampshire has no tax on wage or salary income. Its former Interest and Dividends Tax (which had been phasing down, at 3% for tax year 2024) was fully repealed for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, per NH Department of Revenue Administration Technical Information Release TIR 2025-001. This confirms kind is 'none' outright for 2026 (no bracket table, no flat rate, and no remaining tax on interest/dividend income for individuals), not merely an exemption limited to wages. Every attempt to fetch revenue.nh.gov pages directly (the news-and-media repeal announcement, the TIR 2025-001 PDF itself, the 'taxes-glance' overview, and the interest-and-dividends FAQ) returned HTTP 403 in this session, so the primary source could not be read directly; the repeal date and TIR citation are confirmed via a law firm summary (McLane Middleton) that names the specific TIR number and effective date, corroborated by two independent accounting-firm summaries (Grott Luker; Maloney and Kennedy) found via search, all agreeing on January 1, 2025 as the repeal date. New Hampshire does not operate a mandatory, employee-funded payroll program: its NH PFML program (60% wage replacement up to the SSA wage cap) is voluntary for both employers and employees. Pending 2026 legislation (HB 1761) would create a mandatory, employee-funded Family and Medical Leave Insurance program, but it had not been enacted as of this review, so no payroll program is listed.
sources: https://www.mclane.com/insights/nh-interest-and-dividends-tax-repealed-as-of-january-1/ (law firm summary citing NH DRA Technical Information Release 2025-001; primary revenue.nh.gov pages returned HTTP 403 and could not be read directly)

states.name: Delaware
states.notes: Data is Tax Year 2025 (forms revised 03/26/26, filed by April 30, 2026) — the latest published year as of this research (July 2026); Delaware's brackets and standard deduction are fixed dollar amounts set by statute (30 Del. C. §1102, §1108), not annually inflation-indexed, so no separate 2026 schedule has been or is expected to be issued with different figures. Delaware uses ONE bracket table for all filing statuses (single, MFJ, MFS, HOH) — only the standard deduction differs by status ($6,500 joint vs. $3,250 for single/MFS/HOH). An additional $2,500 standard deduction is allowed per filer age 65+ or blind (not reflected in the base amounts above). Delaware has no employee-side state disability or paid-family-leave payroll tax (payrollPrograms is empty). Separately from the state brackets, the City of Wilmington levies a local wage tax of 1.25% on gross earned income of both residents and nonresidents working within city limits — this is a municipal tax, not part of the state's progressive schedule, and is not folded into the brackets above; confirmed via secondary source (city tax documentation referenced through search), not read directly on a primary Wilmington government page.

states.name: Rhode Island
states.notes: Tax Year 2026 figures, from RI Division of Taxation Advisory ADV 2025-22 (issued Nov 3, 2025), which sets inflation-adjusted brackets/standard deductions effective for tax years beginning on/after Jan 1, 2026 (these appear on returns filed in early 2027, not the 2025 returns filed in 2026). Rhode Island uses ONE 'uniform tax rate schedule' applied to ALL filing statuses (single, MFJ/qualifying widow(er), MFS, HOH) — only the standard deduction and phase-out thresholds differ by status. A personal/dependency exemption of $5,250 per person (2026) also applies on top of the standard deduction (Delaware, by contrast, has no separate exemption amount). Standard deduction and exemption amounts phase out entirely for federal AGI (as RI-modified) between $261,000 and $290,800 for 2026; the phaseout increment is $7,450. TDI rate and wage base are also confirmed for 2026 (effective Jan 1, 2026) via RI Dept. of Labor & Training: rate fell from 1.3% (2025) to 1.1%, while the wage base rose from $89,200 (2025) to $100,000 (2026) per HB 6066. RI's TDI includes the Temporary Caregiver Insurance (TCI) paid-family-leave benefit within the same combined rate/wage base — there is no separate employee-side PFL tax.
